doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Why he collects musician stories: the Local 802 column
summary: He loved musicians' stories and began a column of them in the Local 802 union paper after being elected to the board.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well let me ask you about this book. What prompted you to get into this idea of trying to — this is a mammoth project.

Well I’ll tell you, I’ve always loved musicians’ stories, and it’s been one of the nicest things about hanging out with musicians is that they remember even adversity in humorous terms after the original pain is over. And I used to love to sit around and listen to Roy Eldridge tell stories, and Hot Lips Page and people like that. It would just knock me out that there was such a slice of life there, and usually it was a funny story about somebody else. You know you could rag on somebody to tell about their foibles or weaknesses or some time that they were taken for a fool or whatever. So I can’t imagine how many times I’ve heard, during one of these story sessions, somebody say, boy somebody should write these down, these are great. So about the time I got involved in Local 802, the New York Musician’s Union, the new president, we all got swept in on like a clean slate, I think we got tired of what the old administration was doing. And John Glasel said, “By golly, if I can’t get somebody else to run for president I’ll do it myself” and, “how many of you guys are willing to be on the board?” So only the top four officers had to give up their musical careers in order to be union officials, so I didn’t mind being on the board, and I was willing to run for office. And we were surprised that we all got elected, and none of the old administration was left in at all. So there was a monthly newspaper that the union published, and John was looking for material for it, and he said, “How’d you like to write a column?” And I said, “Yes, I would, and I know exactly the column I’d like to write, I’d like to start of putting some of these musicians stories in there.” So the first six months I guess, I just wrote stuff that I remembered people having told me or things that had happened to me personally.
